strategies.name: Your current rotation
strategies.why: This is the rotation you grow today. The other options are compared against it.

evidence.finding: Groundwater storage in this region has dropped about 1.2 cm per year since 2002.
July and August average highs of 33-34 °C, during corn's flowering and grain fill.

benefits: Strong local market and familiar equipment
Highest income of the three when irrigation water is available
gaps: How much water your well can still deliver
expert_review: Six bare months leave silt loam exposed to spring wind erosion
Irrigation demand peaks when the aquifer is under the most pressure

strategies.name: Keep corn, add a winter cover
strategies.why: Living roots hold the soil through the windy months and build organic matter. The trade-off: the cover crop uses some of the moisture stored over winter.

evidence.finding: Silt loam with 1.6% organic matter: easy to erode when bare, slow to rebuild.
Root-zone soil moisture recovers to 0.46-0.50 between January and May.

benefits: Five fewer months of bare soil
Less wind erosion in March and April
Can be grazed in early spring
gaps: How much stored water the rye uses in a dry spring
expert_review: End the rye early in dry years so corn starts with enough moisture
Check crop insurance rules for cover crop termination dates

strategies.name: Switch to sorghum with a legume cover
strategies.why: Grain sorghum needs less water than corn and handles July heat better. Winter peas fix nitrogen over winter, which can cut fertilizer for the next crop.

evidence.finding: Falling groundwater makes low-water crops a hedge against future pumping limits.
About 59% of the year's rain falls from May to August, matching sorghum's growing season.

gaps: Local sorghum prices and elevator access
Vetch survival in your coldest winters
expert_review: Check that your planter and combine can handle sorghum
Winter peas can become a weed in wheat if they set seed
